prize_parts.citation: for a body of work that renews lyric, essay and narrative through the encounter between ancient and modern writing, with formal invention, intellectual depth and emotional force

statement.case_for: Carson has an unmistakable voice and has changed what a book of poetry can be. Autobiography of Red recasts the Geryon material as a verse novel. Nox turns elegy into a physical, archival object. Her classical learning is part of the imaginative work, not an ornament added to it. Drawing on public knowledge only, her record covers several decades and several forms (lyric, verse novel, essay, drama, translation). The central themes of grief, desire and the limits of language are developed across that record rather than repeated. After reading my colleagues' openings, I still weigh formal and linguistic achievement, depth of imagination and sustained quality in her favour. My second choice, Cărtărescu, is a very strong case on scale and visionary ambition, but I find Carson's formal renewal more distinctive and more durable in its reach across genres.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that much of Carson's work is short, fragmentary or hybrid, and some of it depends on typography and physical design. That makes it hard to compare with large novelistic oeuvres under common criteria. Her translations and scholarship may also blur the line between original achievement and learned craft. A related worry is whether the aggregate corpus has the breadth of reach that a prize for a whole body of work implies. The Nobel will's reference to an idealistic direction is open to interpretation here, and I cannot settle that interpretation from the evidence supplied.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for a recognizable, densely patterned voice and a mature oeuvre. She ranks Carson fifth, asking whether the committee will read Carson as lasting literature or as a scholarly, learned game, and noting that the corpus is mainly short and hybrid.
responses.response: I take the 'learned game' worry seriously, since it is the sharpest form of my own reservation. I would answer that in Nox and Autobiography of Red the scholarship is not a game played above the emotion but the way the emotion is reached. Nox is an elegy for a brother that treats translation as a form of mourning. I agree that Carson's short, hybrid corpus is hard to weigh against Cărtărescu's architectural scale. I think that is a difference of kind, not of quality. I also agree with Mattson that Cărtărescu's rhythmic density may not survive translation fully. That uncertainty applies to Carson's typographic forms as well, so it does not separate the two candidates cleanly.

responses.point: Olsson puts Adonis first on voice, formal achievement and intellectual depth. He notes that translation carries Arabic poetry only partly. He ranks Carson second and says her hybrid forms make comparison with more conventional bodies of work difficult.
responses.response: I agree with Olsson that Adonis's renewal of Arabic poetic language is a major formal and historical achievement, and I ranked him sixth only because of my own limits. I cannot judge Arabic prosody or the weight of his later work from translations. I cannot treat that gap as a point against him, but I also cannot build a preference on a case I cannot assess directly. I share Olsson's caution on Carson's hybrid forms, and the answer is to judge the work on its writing, not on the novelty of hybridity. A citation for her should rest on the poems and on the formal intelligence of the books, with the translations as context.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Carson third. He calls the hybrid forms original, but doubts whether the oeuvre is deep or consistent enough across its many experimental projects. He also says the quality of the smaller, performance-oriented works is uneven.
responses.response: Unevenness among the smaller projects is a fair observation, and I cannot rule it out because I have not independently re-read the works. I would distinguish the peripheral occasional pieces from the core books, where the voice and the formal intelligence are consistent. A citation should rest on that core. I agree that range is not the same as depth, and that is why I would not rest the case on hybridity alone. I read the sustained return to grief, translation and desire as depth, though I accept this is a judgement that colleagues who know the later work better may contest.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson first and Cărtărescu second. She argues that scholarship and poetry become one practice in Carson's work, and she cautions that the citation should not rest on the novelty of hybridity alone. She also notes that Cărtărescu's poetry is thinly covered in translation.
responses.response: I agree with Palm on both counts. The citation I propose names the encounter between ancient and modern writing and the formal invention it produces, so that it does not rest on hybridity as such. On Cărtărescu, I accept her point that the case rests mainly on the prose projects, and I flag that my own knowledge of his poetry is thinner. That is why I treat him as a strong alternative and not as an equal on the evidence available to me.

uncertainties: How far Carson's typographic and physical-object works can be judged in translation, or from reproductions, is unresolved.
I have not independently verified or re-read any of the works. My assessment rests on public knowledge, and I cannot judge the quality of the later work against the best-known books.
How much weight Carson's translations and classical scholarship should carry relative to her original writing is a committee judgement that remains open.

Comparison across very different oeuvres (short hybrid forms, very large novels, poetry in Arabic or Spanish) under common criteria depends heavily on translation coverage, which is uneven and which I cannot measure.
Whether the will's framing favours a body of work with broader social and historical reach than Carson's is a matter of interpretation, and I have not resolved it.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My profile records no connection to any shortlisted writer. It does record that I am a co-opted member, and that whether co-opted members vote in committee is not documented, so my simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
